events.active_fish_man_corridor_01_depar: After living on the island long enough to understand its rhythms, you finally identify a viable window toward the New World. The exact destination will depend on the current available when you leave.
Check the current tables and be ready for the next departure window.

The current tables change. This time, Fish-Man Island no longer feels like a place you merely crossed through: you have had time to live, work, or help someone here. A new departure window is opening toward New World waters.
A Window to the New World
events.active_fish_man_corridor_01_i01_d: The first drop throws you into a frame. A restraint snaps, several people panic, and the descent continues with injuries and a badly broken rhythm.
You read the first shift before it arrives and call the bracing change at exactly the right moment. The descent steadies almost at once.
You catch the line too late. The jolt knocks the breath from you and panic spreads before the craft is steadied.
You ride the drop instead of fighting it. The braces hold and the group quickly finds the rhythm of the descent.
Take the descent line and set the rhythm.
Sabaody’s light narrows above you. Pressure builds, the hull or cabin groans, and the current suddenly pitches everyone forward. The first seconds will decide whether the descent stays controlled.
events.active_fish_man_corridor_01_i02_u: You correct at the wrong moment. The black current slams the side, tears grips loose, and drives you into the deck before the course is barely recovered.
You anticipate where the two currents converge and slip through their seam. The pressure turns into a clean acceleration toward the distant lights of the island.
The correction comes too wide. The transport cuts through a pressure pocket that batters everyone and costs long seconds before the course is recovered.
You follow the darkest vein until the pressure finally eases. The Red Line passes overhead without taking control of the course.
Read the seam in the current and correct at the last moment.

The last natural light disappears. Ahead, two bodies of water cross beneath the Red Line like invisible rivers. A bad correction can pin the transport into the pressure flow; the right one opens the route toward the underwater island.
events.active_fish_man_corridor_01_i03_a: The bubble clears the last dark water and the island’s light fills the horizon. You disembark among the docks, still carrying the crossing in your legs.
Follow the harbor lights and disembark as soon as the passage opens.
You let the pressure equalize in stages. When the exit finally opens, the streets of Fish-Man Island lie ahead and everyone can step onto solid ground.
Take the slow berth and check everyone before disembarking.

After the darkness beneath the Red Line, colors appear in the distance: inhabited reefs, traffic bubbles, and sheltered docks. Only the pressure lock remains before everyone can get back onto solid ground.
events.active_fish_man_corridor_01_local: You open the wrong pocket. The coating snaps, tears you from your footing, and the hull takes the hit before the workers can close the tear.
You also spot a second weakness before it starts flexing. The workers fix both areas at once and credit you with preventing a major repair.
You release the tension too quickly. The repair holds, but the pressure rebound strikes part of the hull.
You find the pocket loading the seam and bleed it in stages. The coating settles back into a clean curve.
Climb up with the crew and bleed the stressed pocket.
You pay for a full hull inspection. The yard returns the ship checked without asking you to take another risk.
Pay for a full inspection and let the specialists work.
Barely docked, a coating worker points out a long milky scar across the hull bubble. One section flexed during the descent and must be relieved before the next pressurization.
A Bubble Pulling Sideways
You mistake a backwash for the end of the sequence. The next surge catches you in the open and throws you against the slope before you can reach shelter.
You spot a weak pulse that signals the true cycle change. The survey becomes more precise than expected and the chartmaker increases your share.
You miss one pulse and have to stay for another cycle. The survey is saved, but the current catches you during the retreat.
You record the full sequence and leave before the next surge. The chartmaker pays you the promised share of the survey.
Read the markers and record the full sequence before the next heavy surge.

A local chartmaker is checking a current that strikes Coral Hill in irregular pulses. The markers are holding, but she needs a second set of eyes to record the sequence without staying exposed too long.
Survey of the Pulses
You reset the ribbons and the buyer realizes nobody will help him expand the cut. The harvesters finish without widening the patch.
Refuse the off-limit cut and reset markers shifted by the current.
You stay inside the markers and help sort what can be taken without ripping out young growth. The harvesters pay you for the work rather than for volume.
Help the harvesters finish the approved patch cleanly.
Harvesters tie ribbons around an approved coral patch while an impatient buyer urges them to cross the markers and fill his baskets faster.
The Marked Harvest
You take the wrong angle. The cable snaps tight, slams both of you into the reef, and the last loop has to be torn free in a panic.
You use the cable itself as a return line. The diver comes free and you climb back together without touching the sharp coral.
You free the diver, but the current throws both of you into the coral before you can climb back toward shelter.
You approach from the sheltered side, loosen the loop, and guide the diver out of the current. They come out with only a few scrapes.
Reach the loop and free it before the current pins the diver against the reef.
At the edge of a Coral Hill drop, a harvester is caught in an old marker cable. Every movement tightens the loop while a side-current pulls them toward sharp coral.
The Diver in the Cable
You repeat their cadence aloud. The group crosses in the right window, and the guides appreciate that you relayed their instructions instead of arguing with them.
Follow the guides’ count and help other travelers leave at the right moment.
The movement of the water feels familiar. You translate what you feel into simple landmarks for the visitors, and the tunnel clears without incident.
Read the water yourself and explain the change to the travelers.
You give up a few minutes. When the push finally weakens, you cross safely without adding to the guides’ workload.
Wait for the current to ease instead of forcing the passage.
At the mouth of a transit tunnel, local guides stop travelers: a cross-current has shifted since morning. Surface visitors hesitate over directions that seem to contradict the signs.
Guides of the Cross-Current
You grab the wrong bale at the wrong angle. Two more slam into you and the ring widens before the handlers can stop it.
You use the current to bring the bales back one behind another. The last one nearly settles itself against the anchor and the plaza applauds the maneuver.
You break the rhythm of the ring, but a bale catches you in the shoulder before the last one is secured.
You work against the pattern instead of meeting it head-on. The bales return to the anchor without hitting a bystander.
Enter the ring and bring the bales back to the anchor one by one.
A bubble cart loses its restraint at the edge of the plaza. Heavy bales drift in a circle around the vehicle, accelerated by a traffic current, and threaten passersby.
The Ring of Cargo Bales
You remove obsolete schedules and group the warnings still in force. The board becomes readable again before the next convoy crowd arrives.
Sort the notices by seal and date before putting them back.
You spend a long while sending groups toward the correct tunnels. When the attendant returns, nobody has followed the old dangerous detour.
Stay at the junction and redirect travelers until an attendant returns.
A traffic bubble bursts against the plaza notice board. Work notices, schedules, and current warnings scatter while travelers are already following outdated directions.
Notices Adrift
You declare the scale rigged too quickly. A second test proves you wrong, the crowd turns, and you have to pay for some of the goods spilled in the argument.
You run three cross-checks using weights from neighboring stalls. The crowd sees exactly where the discrepancy comes from and the merchants adopt the check for the rest of the day.
You restore the weighing but leave everyone to interpret the result. The argument continues and you pay to replace a basket knocked over near you.
You test the counterweight and then the goods. The fault is identified without humiliating either seller or customers, and trading resumes.
Reweigh the goods in front of everyone and force a verifiable result.
Familiar local cues
Two customers accuse a dried-shell vendor of rigging his scale. The vendor swears pressure shifted the counterweight; the crowd starts taking sides before anyone has tested it.
The Vendor’s Scale
You take the map literally and lead the group into a current loop. You have to pay for local transport to get everyone out before someone collapses.
You reconstruct the whole route from the current pulses and show the crew how to read the changes. They leave with a reliable method, not just an escort.
You notice the reversal too late. The detour costs time, energy, and a paid passage to get back onto the correct route.
You correct the arrows against the real flow and find a junction marked from the opposite direction. The crew reaches the docks without another detour.
Re-read the map against the current flow and guide them to the right junction.
A small surface crew missed its guide and no longer knows which tunnel leads back to the docks. Their map shows arrows for the rising flow, but the current has already reversed.
The Crew Without a Current
You cover the disputed handling fee to move the lot immediately. The berth starts flowing again, but your wallet carries the cost of the quick solution.
Front the handling fee to get the crates out of the way.
You match seals, weights, and destinations until the list makes sense again. The handlers clear the queue and thank you for preventing a blanket seizure.
Rebuild the manifest from the marks still visible on the crates.
A surface convoy dropped its crates at the wrong berth after the crossing. Two handlers argue over a soaked manifest while the queue blocks the passage.
Crates Without a Berth
You mistake a real emergency for a panic attack. Trying to recover the mistake leaves you exhausted and hurt in the scramble.
You spot a subtle reaction before it turns dangerous. The clinic reorganizes triage around your observation and several travelers avoid getting worse.
You let a serious case wait a few minutes too long. The medic stabilizes the patient, but the mistake shakes you and takes a physical toll.
You quickly separate emergencies from travelers who are mostly panicking. The medic can focus treatment where it matters.
Help triage the patients and identify signs that need immediate treatment.
In a small harbor clinic, several surface travelers are still shaking after the descent. A medic is short-handed and needs help separating panic from dangerous pressure reactions.
Depth Sickness
You give the loudest people the floor and both lines collapse together. The guards have to push everyone back; you take a hit in the crush and become the target of the complaints.
You turn the crowd into two workable lines and pass information group to group. The gallery starts moving again before the new barrier is fully secured.
You convince part of the group, but not its ringleaders. The gallery stays closed longer and the argument leaves you drained.
You separate the genuinely urgent cases and get everyone else to step back. The guards reopen a narrow lane without another surge.
Calm both lines and secure an orderly passage for urgent cases.
A public gallery is closed after a traffic barrier breaks. Guards are trying to keep two lines apart while a group of travelers insists they will miss their convoy.
The Closed Corridor
The host shows where to leave shoes, bags, and cumbersome weapons. The group stops guessing and the entrance resumes with visible relief.
Simply ask the host what is expected before entering.
You wait a moment, then follow the motions without turning them into a performance. The travelers behind you understand as well and the doorway clears.
Watch local residents enter and follow their sequence.
At the entrance to a meeting house, a group of travelers blocks the way while trying to guess the local etiquette. The hosts wait, somewhere between amusement and impatience.
Sandals at the Entrance
You refuse to turn harbor rumors into official evidence. The clerk grumbles, removes your name from the record, and continues with direct witnesses.
Refuse to sign an account you cannot confirm.
Your testimony narrows the dispute to a few verifiable lots. The clerk redraws the allotment without blaming an entire group for diverting the shipment.
Describe only the cargo and timings you actually saw at the harbor.
Outside a kingdom supply office, cooks and carriers dispute how to divide a shipment delayed by the currents. A clerk asks for precise testimony before redrawing the allotments.
The Supply Hearing
You jam the collar at an angle. The conduit lashes when flow returns, strikes you, and forces the workers to shut the whole section again.
You use the lull to realign the coral support as well. The conduit comes back stable and the workers can reopen the pools immediately.
The collar slips on the first try and the jet hits you before you can reset it. The repair finally holds, but not before a hard blow.
You lock both fasteners during the lull. Flow returns without a leak and the district avoids a longer shutdown.
Help fit the collar during the pressure lull.
A public conduit feeding several pools has split along a coral support. Workers shut the main flow, but residual pressure keeps them from fitting the repair collar.
The Coral Conduit
events.active_sabaody_red_line_passage.c: You force one last inspection of the fastenings and coating bubbles. The descent begins with an extra safety margin.
Inspect every seam before the descent.
You refuse to lose the current window. The lines come free and Sabaody vanishes above the bubble.
Commit to the current now, before it turns.
You shift passengers, bags, and crates until everyone knows where to brace when the sea drops away beneath the hull.
Rebalance people and cargo before casting off.
events.active_sabaody_red_line_passage.t: Preparations are ending on Sabaody. Beneath the mangrove roots, the coating shimmers around the transport that must dive ten thousand meters down. The next current leads under the Red Line; once taken, there will be no dock left to correct a mistake.
